Emma — thanks for the clear asks. We can do both — provide a pro-rata default and an optional three-month smoothing clause as an add-on. I've attached a redlined Order Form (Exhibit B) that includes two alternatives:

A) Monthly pro-rata application (default): tier applied to the prorated usage within the billing month; no retroactive adjustment.
B) 3-month smoothing (optional): new tiers take effect only after a rolling three-month average exceeds the breakpoint threshold; mid-month spikes are credited via a monthly smoothing credit applied on the following invoice.

Practical considerations: B protects against transient spikes but increases exposure for Redwood on sustained high-variance launches. We added an explicit mid-term true-up paragraph and an upper-bound "stabilization cap" for smoothing to limit downside.

I've also uploaded an XLS with the cap-breakpoint ladder and sample calculations so you can model the impact for Beacon's forecast. Links/attachments below. Can you review and confirm which alternative you prefer, or suggest hybrid language? If Beacon goes with smoothing, we'll need a small minimum commit to offset risk (suggested 10% annual committed baseline).

Thanks — I'll loop in Marissa and Aditya for legal/finance redlines.

Best,
Priyom Das
Senior Account Executive | Redwood Inference

Thanks for the ping. I ran the Beacon forecast through the PricingAppendix-CapBreakpoints.xlsx with the sample launch spike scenario. Quick notes:
- If we use monthly pro-rata (A), revenue tracks closely with actual usage but we see potential month-to-month revenue volatility up to ~42% vs. baseline in the first quarter of launch.
- With 3-month smoothing (B) + a 10% committed baseline, initial revenue variance reduces to ~12% but our realized ARR ramps more slowly; operationally that's preferable for Beacon.

Suggested tweak to the smoothing credit: rather than a per-month credit issued the following invoice, use a cumulative quarterly reconciliation to reduce invoice churn. That keeps accounting cleaner for both sides. Also recommend defining an explicit "stabilization cap" percentage (we proposed 150% of the committed baseline) after which additional usage is billed at a short-term premium rate to cover spike risk.

If legal is good with the cap phrasing, finance is comfortable with a 10% baseline and quarterly reconciliation.

-Aditya
Director, Revenue & Pricing | Redwood Inference

Thanks — I reviewed the redline. A few legal points to tighten:
1) Define "Breakpoint" and "Rolling Average" precisely (30/90 day calendar windows rather than "three-month").
2) For the smoothing credit: instead of a term that requires manual crediting, include an automatic reconciliation clause: "If the 90-day rolling average exceeds the Breakpoint, Redwood will apply an invoice-level reconciliation credit equal to the difference between pro-rata invoicing and the applicable tier pricing for the impacted periods, subject to the Stabilization Cap."
3) Stabilization Cap: cap liability to a percentage of invoiced charges or a dollar ceiling (we suggested the greater of 150% of committed baseline or $X,XXX). Use the dollar ceiling when the committed baseline is small.
4) Include an audit right limited to 1x per year to verify usage calculations.

I've attached a tracked-change PDF of Exhibit B with the edits. DocuSign flow should be straightforward once Beacon confirms smoothing vs. pro-rata.

Marissa Cole
Senior Counsel, Commercial Contracts | Redwood Inference
